name: Critical Section Solution Verification (flag/turn-based, Peterson's-style)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek proposed critical-section solution di hai (flag[]/turn variables use karke, jaise Peterson's algorithm ka variant) aur poocha hai ye Mutual Exclusion/Progress/Bounded-Waiting satisfy karta hai ya nahi — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Check all THREE properties explicitly: Mutual Exclusion (two processes in CS together?), Progress (CS empty but a waiting process still blocked unnecessarily?), Bounded Waiting (indefinite postponement possible?).
Try concrete interleavings (process A runs a bit, then B, then A again) to find a counterexample if the solution is flawed.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Trace through a SPECIFIC interleaving of the two (or more) processes' code.
2. Check if mutual exclusion is ever violated (both in CS simultaneously).
3. Check if progress fails (CS free, but no waiting process allowed to enter due to a logic flaw).
4. Check if bounded waiting fails (one process can be perpetually skipped).
5. If all three hold under EVERY possible interleaving, the solution is correct.
variationsObserved: 3-process generalizations of 2-process algorithms (like Peterson's extended to 3) — verify the SAME three properties, often harder to satisfy with more processes.
N-process solutions using a 'max' function or ticket-number scheme (bakery-algorithm-style) — trace the ticket-assignment and ordering logic specifically.
commonTraps: Verifying mutual exclusion but forgetting to separately check progress and bounded waiting — a solution can satisfy ME while failing the other two.

name: Semaphore-Based Classic Problems (Producer-Consumer, Reader-Writer)
recognitionClueHinglish: Producer-Consumer (bounded buffer) ya Reader-Writer problem ka semaphore-based solution diya hai aur poocha hai ye CORRECT hai ya nahi, ya blanks fill karne hain — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Producer-Consumer needs 3 semaphores: mutex(1), empty(N), full(0) — match given code against this template.
Reader-Writer: readcount+mutex (protects readcount) + wrt (writer exclusion, held by first-reader-in/last-reader-out only).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify which semaphores are present and their initial values.
2. Match against the STANDARD template (mutex/empty/full for producer-consumer; readcount/mutex/wrt for reader-writer).
3. Spot any deviation (missing wait/signal, wrong initial value, wrong ordering) that would break correctness.
4. For fill-in-the-blank questions, insert the operation that matches the standard template's role at that point.
variationsObserved: Single binary semaphore reader-writer variant (busy-waiting, simplified) — different from the full readcount+mutex+wrt version, verify against ITS specific simpler correctness requirements.
commonTraps: Swapping the roles of 'empty' and 'full' semaphores (producer should wait on empty/signal full; consumer waits on full/signals empty) — a very common exact-reversal trap.

name: Semaphore Code Trace / Possible Output Values
recognitionClueHinglish: Concurrent processes given semaphores ke saath, aur poocha hai shared variable ki FINAL possible values kya hain, ya ek statement KITNI BAAR print hoga — is topic ka teesra bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: Enumerate the POSSIBLE valid interleavings (respecting each process's own instruction order and any semaphore constraints) — there's usually a RANGE of possible outcomes, not just one.
Look specifically for RACE CONDITIONS (unprotected shared-variable read-modify-write) that allow multiple different final values.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the shared variable(s) and each process's operations on them.
2. Determine which operations are PROTECTED (inside a semaphore-guarded critical section) vs UNPROTECTED (can interleave freely).
3. Enumerate the distinct interleavings of unprotected operations, compute the resulting value for each.
4. Report the count/range of DISTINCT possible final values, or the exact count as asked.
variationsObserved: Multi-threaded lock-based (not pure semaphore) synchronization with non-reentrant locks — reason about deadlock potential if a thread tries to re-acquire its own held lock.
Fetch-and-Add / atomic read-modify-write instructions used directly (no separate lock) — these ARE atomic by definition, so no race condition on that specific operation alone.
commonTraps: Assuming a single deterministic outcome when the code actually allows multiple valid interleavings — always check for genuine race conditions before concluding a unique answer.

name: Test-and-Set / Atomic Instruction Based Mutual Exclusion
recognitionClueHinglish: TEST-AND-SET (ya Fetch-and-Add, ya similar atomic read-modify-write) instruction use karke mutual exclusion implement kiya gaya hai — poocha hai ye CORRECT hai ya nahi, ya kis TYPE ka waiting hai (busy vs blocking).
whatShouldComeToMind: Test-and-Set busy-waits (spinlock) — CPU keeps checking in a loop, doesn't sleep/block.
TAS-based mutex is simple and CORRECT for mutual exclusion, but wastes CPU cycles while waiting — contrast with semaphore's sleep-based blocking.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Recall TAS atomically reads old value AND sets to 1 in one indivisible step — this guarantees only ONE process can successfully 'acquire' at a time.
2. Verify the enter_CS/leave_CS pseudocode correctly loops on TAS until success (enter) and resets the flag (leave).
commonTraps: Assuming TAS-based spinlocks provide FAIRNESS/bounded-waiting automatically — basic TAS loops don't guarantee this without additional mechanism (like a ticket system).

name: Precedence Graph / Fork-Join Concurrent Programming
recognitionClueHinglish: Sequential code diya hai aur poocha hai iska PRECEDENCE GRAPH banao, ya fork/join constructs use karke concurrent program likho jo diye gaye precedence constraints satisfy kare.
whatShouldComeToMind: Precedence graph: nodes=statements, edges=must-happen-before dependencies (based on shared variable read/write dependencies).
Convert to concurrent code using semaphores: one semaphore per edge in the precedence graph, signal() after the source statement, wait() before the destination statement.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Analyze each statement's variable reads/writes, identify true dependencies (a statement reading a variable another writes, must come after).
2. Draw the precedence graph connecting dependent statements.
3. For concurrent-code generation: assign one semaphore per graph edge (initialized to 0), have the SOURCE statement signal() it and the DESTINATION statement wait() on it before executing.
commonTraps: Missing an implicit dependency (two statements both writing the SAME variable, or one reading what another writes) when constructing the graph.

name: Conceptual Definitions (critical section, race condition, classic named problems)
recognitionClueHinglish: Poocha hai 'critical section kya hai', 'race condition kise kehte hain', ya Dining Philosophers jaise classic problems ke deadlock-avoidance techniques — ye definitional/classic-problem pattern hai (52 me se 14 PYQs, sabse bada single cluster).
whatShouldComeToMind: Critical section = code segment accessing SHARED resources, needing mutual exclusion.
Race condition = outcome depends on the RELATIVE TIMING/SPEED of concurrent processes.
Dining Philosophers deadlock avoidance: break circular wait (one philosopher picks up forks in opposite order, or limit concurrent diners to N-1).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Recall the precise definition directly for terminology questions.
2. For Dining-Philosophers-style questions, recall the standard deadlock-avoidance fixes (asymmetric fork order, or resource limiting).
variationsObserved: Barrier synchronization construct definition and analysis (all processes wait until ALL arrive, then all proceed together).
Fork/join process-creation semantics combined with synchronization variable counting.
commonTraps: Confusing 'race condition' with 'deadlock' — race condition is about OUTCOME depending on timing; deadlock is about processes permanently BLOCKED waiting on each other.
